_note: Wine, olive oil and the jars they travel in (Complaint 616, part of 530). Grapes and olives are crops with a stand that takes years to bear; wine and oil are made from them in a press and shipped in amphorae the potter makes. Each figure cites its source in yield_basis or capital_basis (Complaint 656).

grapes_kg.basis: per hectare of bearing vineyard per year, output as kg of grapes at the vintage
grapes_kg.yield_basis: GROWN. The 4000 kg/ha grape yield and the climate classes are the figures the wine entry carried before this split (an unsourced estimate, conf C; the pre-modern unfertilised vineyard it describes). Labour is read from Columella 3.8: that not more than one vinedresser is needed for seven Roman land units (1.766 ha), so one working year (HOURS_PER_PERSON_YEAR, a convention in sim/unit_conversions.py, see Complaints/reports/research-working-year.md, conf C) over those 1.766 ha is about 1132 hours a hectare for the vineyard; the cellar hours are sourced under wine_common_kg. YIELD CHECK: Columella 3.7 reports Graecinus, "setting the lowest estimate", at "twenty amphorae from every iugerum", and 3.11 says vineyards which yield less than three cullei to the iugerum should be rooted out (a culleus is 20 amphorae, Loeb note). At 26 litres an amphora and 2,523 square metres an iugerum that spans about 2000 to 6200 litres of wine a hectare, so the 2700 kg of wine from this entry sits inside the quoted range; the 4000 kg of grapes itself stays an unsourced estimate. LAND: one hectare-year, as in wheat_kg. WAITING YEARS: a new vineyard bears nothing for its first years; that is the `capital` stand below (establishment_years), not a share of this batch. Columella, De Re Rustica 3 (LacusCurtius, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Columella/de_Re_Rustica/3*.html), counts interest over "the two-year period when the vineyards, in their infancy as it were, are delayed in bearing" (section 3.9 of that page). Columella 3.8 sets the labour scale: one vinedresser for seven Roman land units (about 1.8 hectares to one man); the labour above is that figure. YIELD CROSS-CHECK (modern analogue, Complaint 656): Cornell CALS, 'Grapes 101' (https://cals.cornell.edu/news/2021/05/grapes-101-grapes-bottle-of-wine) gives "between two and thirty" tons an acre with "a reasonable average of four tons per acre"; the 4000 kg/ha used here is far below that modern average and inside the Columella range above, as a pre-modern unfertilised vineyard.

capital.good: vineyard stand, one hectare of planted and trained vines
capital.capital_basis: Establishment years: Columella 3.9 as quoted in yield_basis (two years before the vines bear). The land for those two barren years is charged as two hectare-years of hectare_land, spent with the labour. PLANTING LABOUR: Oregon State University Extension EM 8974-E, 'Vineyard Economics: Establishing and Producing Cabernet Sauvignon Wine Grapes in Eastern Oregon' (Julian, Seavert, Kaiser, Skinkis, 2009; PDF opened at https://agsci.oregonstate.edu/sites/agscid7/files/oaeb/pdf/EM8974-E.pdf), Table 7 year-1 establishment hours per acre: mark rows 10.0, mark plants 20.0, plant vines with grow tubes 20.0, tie vines 1.0, vine training 1.0, which is 52 hours an acre, times 2.471 acres a hectare = 128.5 hours a hectare. This is a modern analogue and a LOWER BOUND: it leaves out the machine work (disc, rototill) and any hand trenching of the planting ground (Columella 3.13 and 4 trench the ground to two feet). LIFE: the same publication assumes 'a productive life of 25 years, once full production ... is reached'; a UC extension note (https://lodigrowers.com/vineyard-longevity/) says 'the yield decline is slow, but it accelerates significantly after vineyards are about 15 years old'. 25 years is used. Annual output is the one hectare's bearing yield above.

olives_kg.basis: per hectare of bearing, unirrigated olive grove per year, long-run average across on- and off-bearing years, output as kg of olives
olives_kg.yield_basis: GROWN. Yield from the International Olive Council, 'International olive oil production costs study' (2015; PDF opened at https://www.internationaloliveoil.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/INTERNATIONAL-OLIVE-OIL-PRODUCTION-COSTS-STUDY-.pdf): for system S1, traditional rainfed orchards on steep slopes (fewer than 180 trees/ha, the most common system, 33 percent of the area), oil production is "S1 (370 kg/ha)" and "Processing oil yields average 19.25 per cent"; 370 kg of oil over 19.25 percent is 1922 kg of olives a hectare (the study's own per-country olive yields for S1 run from 730 to 4000 kg/ha). These replace the earlier recalled 1700 kg and 17.6 percent. Labour is read from Cato's staffing as Varro 1.18.1 reports it: an oliveyard of 60.6 ha (240 Roman land units) has "an overseer, a housekeeper, five labourers, three teamsters, one muleteer, one swineherd, one shepherd" (13 slaves). Only the five labourers are counted, one working year each (HOURS_PER_PERSON_YEAR, an engineering estimate, conf D) over those 60.6 ha, about 165 hours a hectare. This is the lower bound: the overseer and housekeeper are overhead (Varro 1.18.3 says they are not clearly counted in the number), and the teamsters, muleteer and herdsmen serve the whole estate, not the grove; counting all 13 would give about 430 hours. Varro 1.18.3 also notes the figures do not scale with farm size. Saserna's one man to eight Roman land units, about 2 ha (1.18.2), is a general rule for land, not for olives, and is not used. Vineyard cross-check: Cato's 25.2 ha vineyard has ten labourers among fifteen slaves (1.18.1), about 790 hours a hectare on the same basis, the same order as the Columella figure (1132) which is kept. The pressing hours are sourced under olive_oil_kg. Varro, De Re Rustica 1.18 (LacusCurtius, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Varro/de_Re_Rustica/1*.html), as used for labour above. KNOWLEDGE (Complaints/531): the tree is an Old World cultigen, gated on mat_olive_oil. LAND: one hectare-year.

capital.good: olive grove stand, one hectare of planted trees
capital.capital_basis: YEARS BEFORE BEARING: Hunker, 'How Long Does It Take For An Olive Tree To Produce Fruit?' (https://www.hunker.com/13428601/how-long-does-it-take-for-an-olive-tree-to-produce-fruit/): olive trees "bear fruit in their fifth year" and reach full yields "seven to eight years after planting"; growables.org (https://growables.org/information/TropicalFruit/OliveArcRFC.htm) says light crops come "after 3 to 4 years"; Olive Oil Times (https://www.oliveoiltimes.com/production/iucn-studies-the-tradeoffs-between-intensive-and-traditional-olive-groves/135545) gives initial production "between three and five years". The model has barren years then full yield, so 5 is taken: four barren years, and a ramp from the fifth to the seventh or eighth year that averages about half a crop (4 + about 1). The barren years' land is charged as five hectare-years of hectare_land. LIFE: Wikipedia, Olive (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olive): "Olive trees can remain productive for centuries as long as they are pruned correctly and regularly", tree-ring and radiocarbon maximum ages 300 to 500 years; 300 years is taken (the lower bound). PLANTING LABOUR: Olive Oil Times (above) gives broadly spaced traditional trees "80 to 120 per hectare", so 100 trees; a grower on the growingfruit.org forum (https://growingfruit.org/t/scared-of-all-the-holes-we-have-to-dig-are-we-crazy-to-take-on-12-trees-at-once/31622?page=2) says "Takes me about 1/2 hour to plant one tree in my rock hard, dry clay soil" and another "maybe 10 minutes per hole"; 100 trees times 0.5 hour = 50 hours a hectare. A modern hobby analogue and a lower bound (it leaves out hauling and staking, and Cato 44 has the foot of each olive dug monthly until it is three years old, which belongs to upkeep). Annual output is the one hectare's bearing yield above.

amphora_count.basis: per hundred empty transport jars (amphorae) of about 26 litres
amphora_count.yield_basis: MADE. The jar is fired earthenware, so its clay and fuel are the ceramic_kg recipe's (clay at the pit, firewood, wheel time); this entry adds the neck, handles and stamp. Capacity: the Roman amphora quadrantal, the standard liquid measure, is "approximately 25.9 L" (Wikipedia, Ancient Roman units of measurement, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Roman_units_of_measurement, which tabulates 26.2 L); a Dressel 20 oil jar averaged 62.83 litres (Peacock and Williams, listed on Roman Inscriptions of Britain, https://romaninscriptionsofbritain.org/instrumentum/2494), so 26 litres is a small standard jar, not the large oil type. The one empty mass found is for another type: a Dressel 20 oil jar (about 70 litres) had an empty weight (tara) of "unos 30 kg" (Aguilera Martin, as cited under olive_oil_kg p. 15); EMPTY MASS: SOURCED. Arthur de Graauw, 'From Amphora to TEU: Journey of a container' (Coastal Engineering and Shiphandling, Grenoble, 22/10/2016; PDF read at https://www.ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/ETUDESarchivees/Containers/Containers1.pdf), section 1 on the amphora quadrantal: "one amphora quadrantal is one Roman cubic foot ... or 26 litres. A full amphora (olive oil, wine, fish sauce) weights around 50 kg, out of which around half is tare", so about 25 kg empty for this 26-litre jar; page 2 gives the Dressel 1B wine jar as "Weight: 24 to 26 kg (empty)" and "Capacity: 24 to 26 l.". The 25 kg used is half of 50 kg and the middle of the 24 to 26 kg range (a secondary conference paper, so conf C for the mass); it replaces 15 kg, and the ceramic_kg input is 100 jars times 25 kg. POTTER HOURS: a blog working back from Monte Testaccio (https://fishandpeaches.blogspot.com/2012/03) assumes "7 pots a day each" at a Dressel 20 workshop (a jar of about 60 litres, built in two sections on the wheel with neck, handles and stamp added), which at an 8-hour day is 1.14 hours a jar, about 114 hours for these 100 smaller jars, neck, handles and stamp included. The ceramic_kg recipe this entry draws on already books 1750 potter hours for 2500 kg of ware (700 hours a tonne in 30_fuel_stone.json), far above 114, so the extra potter hours here are nil (0.0). The ceramic recipe's wheel time overstates the jar against this source by about fifteen times, which is part of why the Rome jar costs so much of the wine it holds (Complaint 656, Also); it is left for the ceramic_kg entry to be revised. The source is an illustrative blog figure, conf C.

wine_common_kg.basis: per hectare of vineyard per year, output as kg of fermented common (table) wine, taking wine's density as close to water's
wine_common_kg.yield_basis: MADE from grapes_kg. Treading and pressing recovers roughly 65-70 percent of the grapes' weight as must, fermentation loses a few percent as CO2, so 4000 kg of grapes gives 2700 kg of wine (the same unsourced estimate the entry carried before, conf C). The wine is stored and shipped in jars: 26 litres to a jar at wine's density near water's is 2700/26 jars, each used once for the first fill: Aguilera Martin (as cited under olive_oil_kg p. 15) says wine jars, unlike oil jars, were reused, but no count of refills exists in any source opened (Pecci et al. 2017, J. Archaeol. Sci. Reports, DOI 10.1016/j.jasrep.2017.02.025, finds wine residue reuse at Oplontis without a count), and Pena (2021) judges the evidence for reuse in the Roman world to be "scattered, uneven, and less than substantial" (https://www.ancientportsantiques.com/ancient-trade/ancient-containers/), so one use is the defensible baseline, conf C. RECOVERY CHECK: Cornell CALS, 'Grapes 101' (https://cals.cornell.edu/news/2021/05/grapes-101-grapes-bottle-of-wine): "Gallons of wine per ton = 130-180", a working figure of 150; at a short ton of 907 kg and 3.785 litres a gallon that is 0.54 to 0.75 litres a kilogram, 0.63 at 150, so the 0.675 used here sits inside. CELLAR LABOUR: WineMaker magazine, 'Scaling up grapes' (https://winemakermag.com/technique/scaling-up-grapes): a home crusher "can process about one ton (900 kg) per hour" and one needs "one or two helpers on crushing day", so about 3 person-hours a tonne to crush; pressing taken as the same again (an assumption, no figure in the source), 4 tonnes times 6 = 24 hours a hectare. PRESS: Cato, De Agricultura 11 (LacusCurtius, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Cato/De_Agricultura/A*.html), equips a vineyard of 25.2 ha with "3 complete presses"; one press serves a third of that, 8.41 ha (at 2,523 square metres to the Roman land unit, Wikipedia as above), so its yearly capacity is that area times the 2700 kg/ha. Press timber and stone are now read from Cato 18 and 19 (see capital_basis); build labour is under capital_basis; the press life is under capital_basis.

capital.good: wine press, beam press with its pressing floor
capital.capital_basis: Capacity from Cato 11: 3 presses to 25.2 ha (see yield_basis), 8.41 ha each, at 2700 kg of wine a hectare. Cato, De Agricultura 18 (LacusCurtius, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Cato/De_Agricultura/A*.html): "Anchor-posts 2 feet thick, 9 feet high, including tenons"; "guide-posts 2 feet in diameter and 10 feet high, including the tenons"; "cover the whole area 5 feet by 2½ feet with hard stones to a depth of 1½ feet"; "lay on it a flat stone, 2½ by 2½ by 1½ feet, and set the posts on it". Roman foot 296 mm (Wikipedia, Ancient Roman units of measurement, "Using the value 296 mm (11.7 in) for the Roman foot"), so a cubic foot is 0.0259 cubic metres. Counted per press: two anchor-posts taken as 2 by 2 feet square in section, two guide-posts round, one anchor foundation block and two guide-post flat stones, which is 4.24 cubic metres of timber and 37.5 cubic feet (0.973 cubic metres) of stone; stone at 2650 kg per cubic metre (Wikipedia, Granite: average density between 2.65 and 2.75 g/cm3; Cato says only 'hard stones'), 2577 kg. These are LOWER BOUNDS: Cato gives no section for the press-beam, windlass or levers, and the pavement, press seat and mill stones are not totalled, and the square section of the anchor-posts is an assumption (conf C for the counted parts). Wine press (Cato 19 raises the guide-posts and anchor-posts two feet: 11 and 12 feet). CARPENTER HOURS: a hobby timber framer on permies.com (https://permies.com/t/58723/Hand-hewing-beams) hews "about 4 hours per 12 foot beam"; with the 7.5 by 7.5 inch section another poster on that page gives for uprights, a 12 foot beam is 0.1905 x 0.1905 x 3.658 = 0.133 cubic metres, so 30.1 hours a cubic metre of hewing, times 4.24 cubic metres = 127.6 hours (hewing only, joinery not counted: a lower bound). MASON HOURS: Building Construction Vol. IV, Data on Rubble Masonry (https://chestofbooks.com/architecture/Building-Construction-V4/Data-On-Rubble-Masonry.html): per perch of 25 cubic feet, 1/3 day of mason and 1/4 day of helper; at an 8-hour day that is 6.6 hours a cubic metre. The masonry volume is Cato 18's foundations: anchor foundation 5 x 2.5 x 5 feet, two guide-post foundations 2.5 x 2.5 x 5 feet and the press seat 6 feet across and 5 deep (circular), 266 cubic feet or 6.9 cubic metres, so 45.5 hours. LIFE: a Burgundy winemaker's forum post (Wine Berserkers, 'Renovating old Burgundian winery vertical press', https://www.wineberserkers.com/t/renovating-old-burgundian-winery-vertical-press/82956) describes a "19th century vertical wine press" that "functioned perfectly" at the 2013 harvest after its oak cage staves were replaced and the hoops repainted, so an oak press frame survived well over 100 years with only its wearing staves renewed; 100 years is taken (the staves' renewal, a small timber cost, is not charged).

olive_oil_kg.basis: per hectare of mature olive grove per year, long-run average, output as kg of pressed oil
olive_oil_kg.yield_basis: MADE from olives_kg. 1922 kg of olives at 19.25 percent recovery is 370 kg of oil (International Olive Council, International olive oil production costs study, 2015, S1 traditional rainfed system: "Processing oil yields average 19.25 per cent" and 370 kg oil/ha; PDF https://www.internationaloliveoil.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/INTERNATIONAL-OLIVE-OIL-PRODUCTION-COSTS-STUDY-.pdf). Oil is held in jars of 26 litres, filled at oil's density, specific gravity 0.911 at 20 C (Wikipedia, Olive oil infobox, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olive_oil), so 26 litres hold 23.7 kg and 370 kg of oil fills 15.62 jars, each used once: oil jars were not refilled, "constituir envases no reutilizables" because the oil soaked the ceramic and went rancid (Aguilera Martin, Evolucion de los tituli picti de las anforas Dressel 20, Acta XII Congressus Internationalis Epigraphiae Graecae et Latinae, p. 15), and the Dressel 20 jars were discarded at Monte Testaccio rather than recycled (Wikipedia, Monte Testaccio, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Testaccio). PRESSING LABOUR: Pliny, Natural History 15.6 (Bostock and Riley, Perseus, https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.02.0137%3Abook%3D15%3Achapter%3D6): a factus is "one hundred modii" and "Four men, working at two presses day and night, ought to be able to press out three factuses of olives"; a modius is 8.73 L (Wikipedia, Ancient Roman units of measurement) and loose olives have a bulk density of about 591 to 647 kg per cubic metre (Determination of some physical properties of virgin olive fruits, CIGR Journal, https://cigrjournal.org/index.php/Ejounral/article/view/2308), 0.62 taken, so 300 modii are 2619 L x 0.62 = 1624 kg; four men for 24 hours is 96 person-hours, 0.059 hours a kilogram, times 1922 kg = 114 hours a hectare. PRESS: Cato 10 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Cato/De_Agricultura/A*.html) equips an oliveyard of 60.6 ha with "5 complete oil-pressing equipments", so a press serves 12.1 ha (240 Roman land units over 5, at 2,523 square metres each; Wikipedia, as in amphora_count), and its yearly capacity is that area times 370 kg/ha. Press timber and stone are read from Cato 18 (see capital_basis); build labour is under capital_basis; the press life is under capital_basis.

capital.good: oil press, beam press with mill and settling vats
capital.capital_basis: Capacity from Cato 10: 5 presses to 60.6 ha (12.1 ha each) at 370 kg of oil a hectare. Cato, De Agricultura 18 (LacusCurtius, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Cato/De_Agricultura/A*.html): "Anchor-posts 2 feet thick, 9 feet high, including tenons"; "guide-posts 2 feet in diameter and 10 feet high, including the tenons"; "cover the whole area 5 feet by 2½ feet with hard stones to a depth of 1½ feet"; "lay on it a flat stone, 2½ by 2½ by 1½ feet, and set the posts on it". Roman foot 296 mm (Wikipedia, Ancient Roman units of measurement, "Using the value 296 mm (11.7 in) for the Roman foot"), so a cubic foot is 0.0259 cubic metres. Counted per press: two anchor-posts taken as 2 by 2 feet square in section, two guide-posts round, one anchor foundation block and two guide-post flat stones, which is 3.50 cubic metres of timber and 37.5 cubic feet (0.973 cubic metres) of stone; stone at 2650 kg per cubic metre (Wikipedia, Granite: average density between 2.65 and 2.75 g/cm3; Cato says only 'hard stones'), 2577 kg. These are LOWER BOUNDS: Cato gives no section for the press-beam, windlass or levers, and the pavement, press seat and mill stones are not totalled, and the square section of the anchor-posts is an assumption (conf C for the counted parts). Oil press (Cato 18, 9 and 10 feet). CARPENTER HOURS: as under wine_common_kg, 30.1 hours a cubic metre of hewing times 3.5 cubic metres = 105.4 hours. MASON HOURS: as under wine_common_kg, 45.5 hours for Cato 18's foundations. LIFE: a Burgundy winemaker's forum post (Wine Berserkers, 'Renovating old Burgundian winery vertical press', https://www.wineberserkers.com/t/renovating-old-burgundian-winery-vertical-press/82956) describes a "19th century vertical wine press" that "functioned perfectly" at the 2013 harvest after its oak cage staves were replaced and the hoops repainted, so an oak press frame survived well over 100 years with only its wearing staves renewed; 100 years is taken (the staves' renewal, a small timber cost, is not charged).
